::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: GBA1 variants are major Parkinson's disease risk factors, but their detection is challenging.
We compared NeuroBooster Array (NBA) genotyping with reference sequencing in 3,744 individuals.
NBA correctly identified 520/608 carriers (85.5%).
Of 89 missed calls, 73 had no matching probe and 16 had missing calls. 25 participants had false positive calls.
NBA should not be used alone for clinical decisions, but is very useful for large case control analysis.
Table 1).
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: GBA1 variants were detected in 608 participants (16.2%): 294 (14.4%) PD cases, 306 non-PD (18.9%), and 8 "Others" (9.2%).
Allele frequencies (AF) are reported in Supplementary Table 2.
text.formatted: Allele frequencies (AF) are reported in Supplementary Table <ref type="table">2</ref>.

text.text: These AF should be interpreted considering the different recruitment strategies and enrichment for GBA1 carriers in the three cohorts.
Across the region of interest, NBA contained 423 probes, covering 316 unique genomic positions (Supplementary Table 3).
text.formatted: Across the region of interest, NBA contained 423 probes, covering 316 unique genomic positions (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">3</ref>).

text.text: Of the 608 carriers identified using reference sequencing, 520 (85.5%) were correctly detected using NBA genotype data.

The 88 GBA1 variant carriers who were not correctly identified with NBA (14.5% of all variant carriers and 2.4% of the whole cohort) accounted for 89 missed variant calls: 73 involved variants for which NBA had no probe targeting the variant allele (Supplementary Table 4), and 16 had a matching probe that returned no call in that individual.
text.formatted: The 88 GBA1 variant carriers who were not correctly identified with NBA (14.5% of all variant carriers and 2.4% of the whole cohort) accounted for 89 missed variant calls: 73 involved variants for which NBA had no probe targeting the variant allele (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">4</ref>), and 16 had a matching probe that returned no call in that individual.

text.text: No carrier was missed when a matching probe returned a call.

Across all NBA probes targeting protein-altering or canonical splice-site changes in the GBA1 region, NBA reported false positive calls in 25 participants (0.7% of all samples analysed), involving 17 variants (Supplementary Table 5).
text.formatted: Across all NBA probes targeting protein-altering or canonical splice-site changes in the GBA1 region, NBA reported false positive calls in 25 participants (0.7% of all samples analysed), involving 17 variants (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">5</ref>).

text.text: In 9 of these 25 participants, the false positive call was made concordantly by all two or three probes targeting the variant.
The best probe for each variant is reported in Table 1 and detailed metrics for each probe targeting the variants in our analysis panel are in Supplementary Table 6.
text.formatted: The best probe for each variant is reported in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> and detailed metrics for each probe targeting the variants in our analysis panel are in Supplementary Table <ref type="table">6</ref>.

text.text: Notably, the best probe for p.N409S (chr1:155235843:T:C), based on sensitivity, false positives, coverage and missingness, was not able to identify any of the 18 homozygous carriers (which were reported as heterozygotes), while another probe with poorer overall performance (ilmnseq_rs76763715.1_F2BT) was able to correctly call 17 of them.
No probe identified the single p.E365K homozygote present in the dataset.

Access to sequencing and genotyping resources is instrumental in advancing our understanding of PD, and GP2 has enabled unprecedented access to genetic information from different populations across the world.
In this work, we show that NBA can correctly detect 85.5% of GBA1 carriers, confirming its value for high-volume case-control analysis.
On the other hand, a proportion of GBA1 carriers were missed (14.5% of all GBA1 variant carriers and 2.4% of the whole cohort).
Most variants are missed because dedicated probes were not included in the current genotyping array design, but some samples also have missing calls due to underperforming probes.
When a probe targeting the correct allele returned a call, no carrier was missed.
Our cohort included mainly individuals of European and Ashkenazi Jewish ancestries and had a relatively high prevalence of p.N409S carriers.
The NBA probes for p.N409S showed an excellent performance overall, so it is possible that the rate of missed variants in an unselected PD cohort might be higher.

Notably, most of the variants missed in our cohort are p.L483P, the most common severe GBA1 variant in Europeans and Asians, and the intronic variant rs3115534-G, the principal African-ancestry GBA1 PD risk variant 8 .
text.formatted: Notably, most of the variants missed in our cohort are p.L483P, the most common severe GBA1 variant in Europeans and Asians, and the intronic variant rs3115534-G, the principal African-ancestry GBA1 PD risk variant <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8</ref> .

text.text: Missing these two variants has significant implications for studies estimating the impact of GBA1 variants on PD pathogenesis.

The potential for mislabelling participants also precludes the use of genotyping with NBA or similar for patient stratification in interventional studies, and clinicians with access to NBA data from study participants should refrain from diagnosing GBA1 status based on NBA alone.
We provide metrics for all probes targeting the variants in our analysis panel and define the best probe for each variant.
In most cases, the difference between probes is trivial, but on large datasets small differences in sensitivity and specificity might produce significant effects.
False positive calls were rare, but in nine participants they were supported by all probes targeting the variant.
For these variants, we cannot exclude miscalling by the reference method.
Several NBA probes share a genomic position with a clinically relevant GBA1 variant but test a different allele, and some rsIDs (e.g. rs104886460) are multiallelic.
Matching probes to . variants by position or rsID alone can therefore attribute calls to the wrong variant.
This highlights that probes should be matched on position and alleles, accounting for strand.
In addition, for 24 custom NBA probes, the position and alleles reported in the released data correspond to a different change from that indicated by the probe name (e.g.
GBA_G232E is reported at c.694, p.G232R, rather than c.695, p.G232E).
The p.G232E and p.L500P carriers in our cohort were called homozygous reference by these probes (Supplementary Table 7).
text.formatted: The p.G232E and p.L500P carriers in our cohort were called homozygous reference by these probes (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">7</ref>).

text.text: Another important point is the rate of variants not called due to missingness, despite a QC step to exclude samples with missingness above 5%.
This is because genome-wide call-rate QC does not protect against locus-specific genotyping failure.
The detection of p.N409S requires a specific mention.
Only one probe correctly identified the majority of p.N409S homozygotes, but another probe had slightly better overall performance (when sensitivity was calculated as a presence/absence metric).
Relying on one or the other probe depends on whether one wants to prioritise high sensitivity or enable the detection of p.N409S homozygotes.
In our analysis, we did not include imputed data.
In certain populations, the intronic variant rs3115534-G, p.E365K and p.T408M can be imputed from NBA (as opposed to p.L483P), so imputation may improve overall detection of GBA1 variants.
GP2 now also includes a substantial volume of WGS data, which, when properly analysed using Gauchian, can detect most or all GBA1 variants.
We encourage researchers using GP2 data to acknowledge the limitations of NBA when genotyping GBA1 and to consider validating their findings or using WGS data whenever possible.
All cohorts had NBA genotyping available through GP2, with each cohort using a distinct reference method to validate GBA1 variant calls.

DNA was used for targeted whole-gene GBA1 sequencing with Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ON), as previously described 9 .

text.text: Samples with genotype missingness above 5% across the full genotyping array content were excluded.
NBA calls were obtained from GP2 Release 11 and analysis was carried out on Verily Workbench.
The GBA1 region of interest (including the 39 amino acid leader peptide) was defined as NC_000001.11:g.155234452_155244627.
Only exonic variants, splicing variants and the known pathogenic intronic variant rs3115534-G were included in this analysis.
Synonymous variants were excluded and carriers of synonymous variants were considered as wild type.
The analysis panel comprised all variants identified by the reference methods plus additional known pathogenic GBA1 variants with NBA probes (Supplementary Table 6).

text.text: Sensitivity, specificity and precision were calculated per probe on non-missing calls.

When more than one probe was available for each variant, the best probe was defined using a four-level ranking, applied in order: highest sensitivity, fewest false positives, most coverage, fewest missing.

False positives were assessed at all NBA probes in the region targeting missense, nonsense, canonical splice-site (±1-2 bp) or coding indel changes, by annotating each probe from its position and alleles (GRCh38, NM_000157.4).

Each probe was evaluated on all participants with a non-missing call: true positives (TP) and false negatives (FN) were participants carrying the variant according to the reference methods who were called non-reference or reference by the probe, respectively; false positives (FP) and true negatives (TN) were non-carriers called non-reference or reference.
Sensitivity was calculated as TP/(TP+FN), specificity as TN/(TN+FP) and precision as TP/(TP+FP).
Carrier detection was assessed per participant and variant.
No statistical tests were performed.
